claim: C. elegans shows food-associated behavioral plasticity in combination with gustatory, olfactory, thermosensory, and mechanosensory cues.
source: C. elegans shows food-associated behavioral plasticity in combination with various sensory modalities including gustatory, olfactory, thermosensory, and mechanosensory cues (Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kindt et al., 2007; Saeki et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Colbert and Bargmann, 1995; Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Kindt et al., 2007; Saeki et al., 2001).

claim: C. elegans shows plasticity in chemotaxis to salt (sodium chloride; NaCl).
source: We have previously reported that C. elegans shows plasticity in chemotaxis to salt (sodium chloride; NaCl); wild-type animals are attracted to the salt concentration at which they have been fed, while avoid the concentrations at which they have been starved (salt concentration chemotaxis, Kunitomo et al., 2013, Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Kunitomo et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Wild-type animals are attracted to the salt concentration at which they have been fed.
source: wild-type animals are attracted to the salt concentration at which they have been fed, while avoid the concentrations at which they have been starved (salt concentration chemotaxis, Kunitomo et al., 2013, Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Kunitomo et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 1a showing experimental data.

claim: Wild-type animals avoid the salt concentrations at which they have been starved.
source: wild-type animals are attracted to the salt concentration at which they have been fed, while avoid the concentrations at which they have been starved (salt concentration chemotaxis, Kunitomo et al., 2013, Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation (Kunitomo et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 1a showing experimental data.

claim: C. elegans senses inorganic ions mainly through the bilateral salt-sensing neuron pair, ASE.
source: C. elegans senses inorganic ions mainly through the bilateral salt-sensing neuron pair, ASE (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Bargmann and Horvitz, 1991).

claim: Sensory input to ASE-right (ASER) is essential and sufficient for food-associated salt chemotaxis.
source: Sensory input to ASE-right (ASER) is essential and sufficient for food-associated salt chemotaxis.
evidence: The claim is stated as an established fact in the introduction, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: The interneurons postsynaptic to ASER, namely, AIA, AIB, and AIY, regulate exploratory behaviors.
source: The interneurons postsynaptic to ASER, namely, AIA, AIB, and AIY, regulates exploratory behaviors (Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2014; Piggott et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2014; Piggott et al., 2011).

claim: Modulation of synaptic transmission between ASER and AIA, AIB, and AIY interneurons is involved in modification of salt chemotaxis.
source: Modulation of synaptic transmission between ASER and these interneurons is involved in modification of salt chemotaxis (Kunitomo et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kunitomo et al., 2013; Luo et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017).

claim: A receptor-type guanylyl cyclase GCY-22 (also known as CHE-5) plays a pivotal role in perception of salt stimuli.
source: A receptor-type guanylyl cyclase GCY-22 (also known as CHE-5) plays a pivotal role in perception of salt stimuli and is suggested to act as an ion receptor of ASER (Adachi et al., 2010; Kunitomo and Iino, 2020; Ortiz et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Adachi et al., 2010; Kunitomo and Iino, 2020; Ortiz et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013).

claim: GCY-22 is suggested to act as an ion receptor of ASER.
source: A receptor-type guanylyl cyclase GCY-22 (also known as CHE-5) plays a pivotal role in perception of salt stimuli and is suggested to act as an ion receptor of ASER (Adachi et al., 2010; Kunitomo and Iino, 2020; Ortiz et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Adachi et al., 2010; Kunitomo and Iino, 2020; Ortiz et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013).

claim: Excitation of ASER depends on cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels consisting of TAX-2 and TAX-4.
source: Excitation of ASER depends also on cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels consisting of TAX-2 and TAX-4 (Suzuki et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Suzuki et al., 2008).

claim: C. elegans genome does not contain typical voltage-gated sodium channel genes.
source: C. elegans genome does not contain typical voltage-gated sodium channel genes (Goodman et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Goodman et al., 1998).

claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels are responsible for propagation of depolarization in C. elegans.
source: Instead, voltage-gated calcium channels are responsible for propagation of depolarization, which is examined by electrophysiological studies (Goodman et al., 1998; Shindou et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Goodman et al., 1998; Shindou et al., 2019).

claim: Contribution of anions to the regulation of ASER activity has not been discussed yet.
source: However, contribution of anions to the regulation of ASER activity has not been discussed yet.
evidence: The claim is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: ClC proteins transport univalent anions across membranes to control electrochemical potential of excitable cells.
source: ClC proteins transport univalent anions across membranes to control electrochemical potential of excitable cells and to maintain ionic milieu as well as pH of intracellular organelles (Ahnert-Hilger and Jahn, 2011; Bösl et al., 2001; Branicky et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ahnert-Hilger and Jahn, 2011; Bösl et al., 2001; Branicky et al., 2014).

claim: ClC proteins maintain ionic milieu as well as pH of intracellular organelles.
source: ClC proteins transport univalent anions across membranes to control electrochemical potential of excitable cells and to maintain ionic milieu as well as pH of intracellular organelles (Ahnert-Hilger and Jahn, 2011; Bösl et al., 2001; Branicky et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ahnert-Hilger and Jahn, 2011; Bösl et al., 2001; Branicky et al., 2014).

claim: Malfunction of ClC genes result in various diseases such as myotonia, leukodystrophy, hyperaldosteronism, and epilepsy in humans.
source: Malfunction of ClC genes result in various diseases such as myotonia, leukodystrophy, hyperaldosteronism, and epilepsy in humans (Blanz et al., 2007; Charlet-B et al., 2002; Fernandes-Rosa et al., 2018; Yamamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Blanz et al., 2007; Charlet-B et al., 2002; Fernandes-Rosa et al., 2018; Yamamoto et al., 2015).

claim: CLH-1 shares the highest (37%) identity with mammalian ClC-2.
source: CLH-1 shares the highest (37%) identity with mammalian ClC-2.
evidence: The claim is stated as a fact based on sequence comparison.

claim: Both CLH-1 and ClC-2 are inwardly rectifying chloride channels.
source: Functional studies using heterologous expression in Xenopus oocytes and mammalian cells demonstrated that both CLH-1 and ClC-2 are inwardly rectifying chloride channels (Grant et al., 2015; Nehrke et al., 2000; Staley et al., 1996; Thiemann et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Grant et al., 2015; Nehrke et al., 2000; Staley et al., 1996; Thiemann et al., 1992).

claim: ClC-2 contributes to Cl− influx in neurons depending on the electrochemical potential of Cl−.
source: On the other hand, two recent studies showed that ClC-2 contributes to Cl− influx in neurons depending on the electrochemical potential of Cl− (Ratté and Prescott, 2011; Rinke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ratté and Prescott, 2011; Rinke et al., 2010).

claim: Two mutants, JN572 and JN577, showed defective chemotaxis toward low salt after feeding on NaCl-free nematode growth medium.
source: Two mutants, JN572 and JN577, showed a similar phenotype: an unbiased salt preference after feeding on NaCl-free nematode growth medium (hereinafter referred to as cultivation at 0 mM NaCl).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: JN572 and JN577 showed normal chemotaxis to high salt after feeding on NGM with 100 mM NaCl.
source: Chemotaxis to high salt after feeding on NGM with 100 mM NaCl (hereinafter referred to as cultivation at 100 mM NaCl), and chemotaxis after starvation were comparable to those of wild-type animals (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: JN572 and JN577 showed normal chemotaxis after starvation.
source: Chemotaxis to high salt after feeding on NGM with 100 mM NaCl (hereinafter referred to as cultivation at 100 mM NaCl), and chemotaxis after starvation were comparable to those of wild-type animals (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Neither shortened nor extended cultivation at 0 mM NaCl ameliorated the defects in JN572 and JN577 mutants.
source: Neither shortened nor extended cultivation at 0 mM NaCl did not ameliorate the defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e), suggesting that the impaired chemotaxis is not due to the delay of behavioral modification.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e.

claim: The impaired chemotaxis in JN572 and JN577 is not due to the delay of behavioral modification.
source: Neither shortened nor extended cultivation at 0 mM NaCl did not ameliorate the defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e), suggesting that the impaired chemotaxis is not due to the delay of behavioral modification.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that varying cultivation time did not affect the phenotype.

claim: The JN572 and JN577 mutants were unable to generate migration bias toward low salt.
source: Rather, the mutants were unable to generate migration bias toward low salt.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing unbiased salt preference.

claim: The mutants showed a preference for high salt after cultivation at 50 mM NaCl.
source: Consistent with this idea, the mutants showed a preference for high salt after cultivation at 50 mM NaCl, under which condition wild-type animals showed an unbiased salt preference (Figure 1b, and see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Wild-type animals showed an unbiased salt preference after cultivation at 50 mM NaCl.
source: Consistent with this idea, the mutants showed a preference for high salt after cultivation at 50 mM NaCl, under which condition wild-type animals showed an unbiased salt preference (Figure 1b, and see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Mutations in JN572 and JN577 were mapped between genetic positions 2.82 and 6.12 (cM) on chromosome II.
source: We mapped mutations of JN572 and JN577 between genetic positions 2.82 and 6.12 (cM) on chromosome II (see Materials and methods, Fay and Bender, 2006; Wicks et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic mapping data and citations (Fay and Bender, 2006; Wicks et al., 2001).

claim: JN572 and JN577 carried a distinct missense mutation in the clh-1 gene.
source: Genome sequencing revealed that they carried a distinct missense mutation in the clh-1 gene, one of six ClC channels/transporters in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is supported by genome sequencing data.

claim: The mutation in JN572 predicted M293I substitution in CLH-1A.
source: Mutations predicted M293I and I146T substitutions in CLH-1A in JN572 and JN577, respectively, and they are hereinafter referred to as clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome sequencing data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: The mutation in JN577 predicted I146T substitution in CLH-1A.
source: Mutations predicted M293I and I146T substitutions in CLH-1A in JN572 and JN577, respectively, and they are hereinafter referred to as clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome sequencing data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: Salt chemotaxis defects of the mutants were recovered by a clh-1(wt) genomic fragment.
source: Salt chemotaxis defects of the mutants were recovered by a clh-1(wt) genomic fragment, confirming that clh-1 is the responsible gene, although the effect was partial in clh-1(pe577) (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: clh-1 is the responsible gene for the salt chemotaxis defects in JN572 and JN577.
source: Salt chemotaxis defects of the mutants were recovered by a clh-1(wt) genomic fragment, confirming that clh-1 is the responsible gene, although the effect was partial in clh-1(pe577) (Figure 1c).
evidence: The claim is confirmed by rescue experiments showing that clh-1(wt) genomic fragment restores the phenotype.

claim: Extra copies of clh-1(wt) genomic fragment weakened low-salt chemotaxis of wild type.
source: We also noticed that extra copies of clh-1(wt) genomic fragment weakened low-salt chemotaxis of wild type (Figure 1c), implying that overexpression of CLH-1 could disrupt chemotaxis to low salt.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Overexpression of CLH-1 could disrupt chemotaxis to low salt.
source: We also noticed that extra copies of clh-1(wt) genomic fragment weakened low-salt chemotaxis of wild type (Figure 1c), implying that overexpression of CLH-1 could disrupt chemotaxis to low salt.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that extra copies of clh-1(wt) weakened low-salt chemotaxis.

claim: Deletion mutants of clh-1 showed almost no discernible defect in salt chemotaxis.
source: Interestingly, deletion mutants of clh-1, all of which harbor a lesion in the pore-forming transmembrane domain of CLH-1 and hence are putative loss-of-function alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a), showed almost no discernible defect in salt chemotaxis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e.

claim: Deletion mutants of clh-1 are putative loss-of-function alleles.
source: Interestingly, deletion mutants of clh-1, all of which harbor a lesion in the pore-forming transmembrane domain of CLH-1 and hence are putative loss-of-function alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a), showed almost no discernible defect in salt chemotaxis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the fact that the deletions affect the pore-forming transmembrane domain.

claim: Chemotaxis defects of clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) were caused by an anomalous activity of clh-1.
source: These results suggest that chemotaxis defects of clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) were caused by an anomalous activity of clh-1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that deletion mutants show no defect while missense mutants do.

claim: clh-1(pe572)/clh-1(wt) and clh-1(pe577)/clh-1(wt) showed normal low-salt chemotaxis.
source: clh-1(pe572)/clh-1(wt) and clh-1(pe577)/clh-1(wt) showed normal low-salt chemotaxis, demonstrating that both missense alleles are recessive to wild-type allele (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Both clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) missense alleles are recessive to wild-type allele.
source: clh-1(pe572)/clh-1(wt) and clh-1(pe577)/clh-1(wt) showed normal low-salt chemotaxis, demonstrating that both missense alleles are recessive to wild-type allele (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is demonstrated by the normal phenotype of heterozygotes.

claim: The effect of both missense alleles are dosage-dependent.
source: Also, we noted that the effect of both missense alleles are dosage-dependent, that is, clh-1(pe572)/clh-1(tm1243) and clh-1(pe577)/clh-1(tm1243) showed a modest defect in salt chemotaxis to low salt after cultivation at 0 mM NaCl (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: clh-1(pe572)/clh-1(tm1243) and clh-1(pe577)/clh-1(tm1243) showed a modest defect in salt chemotaxis to low salt after cultivation at 0 mM NaCl.
source: Also, we noted that the effect of both missense alleles are dosage-dependent, that is, clh-1(pe572)/clh-1(tm1243) and clh-1(pe577)/clh-1(tm1243) showed a modest defect in salt chemotaxis to low salt after cultivation at 0 mM NaCl (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b.

claim: clh-1(tm1243) conferred a weak resistance to an acetylcholine receptor agonist, levamisole.
source: Furthermore, we unexpectedly found that clh-1(tm1243) conferred a weak resistance to an acetylcholine receptor agonist, levamisole.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c.

claim: clh-1(pe572) or clh-1(pe577) caused an enhanced sensitivity to levamisole if compared with wild type.
source: On the contrary, clh-1(pe572) or clh-1(pe577) caused an enhanced sensitivity to levamisole if compared with wild type, suggesting these alleles may not be simple reduction-of-function alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c.

claim: clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) may not be simple reduction-of-function alleles.
source: On the contrary, clh-1(pe572) or clh-1(pe577) caused an enhanced sensitivity to levamisole if compared with wild type, suggesting these alleles may not be simple reduction-of-function alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the opposite effects on levamisole sensitivity compared to the deletion allele.

claim: clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) are recessive mutations whose salt chemotaxis phenotype appears in a dosage-dependent manner.
source: Together, these data show that clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) (hereinafter collectively referred to as clh-1(pe)) are recessive mutations whose salt chemotaxis phenotype appears in a dosage-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the genetic characterization data.

claim: Overexpression of clh-1(pe) conferred defects in low-salt chemotaxis in both wild type and clh-1(tm1243) mutants.
source: Overexpression of mutant clh-1 conferred defects in low-salt chemotaxis in both genomic backgrounds, demonstrating that excess clh-1(pe) override the canonical clh-1(wt) function (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3d.

claim: Excess clh-1(pe) override the canonical clh-1(wt) function.
source: Overexpression of mutant clh-1 conferred defects in low-salt chemotaxis in both genomic backgrounds, demonstrating that excess clh-1(pe) override the canonical clh-1(wt) function (Figure 1—figure supplement 3d).
evidence: The claim is demonstrated by the ability of overexpressed clh-1(pe) to cause defects even in wild-type background.

claim: Excess clh-1, either wild-type or pe alleles, can impair low-salt chemotaxis.
source: Therefore, excess clh-1, either wild-type or pe alleles, can impair low-salt chemotaxis.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the overexpression experiments.

claim: clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) are atypical neomorphic alleles that disrupt chemotaxis to low salt after cultivation at 0 mM NaCl.
source: We concluded that clh-1(pe572) and clh-1(pe577) are atypical neomorphic alleles that disrupt chemotaxis to low salt after cultivation at 0 mM NaCl.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the genetic characterization and overexpression experiments.

claim: All ClC anion channels/transporters characterized so far function as either homodimers or heterodimers.
source: All ClC anion channels/transporters characterized so far function as either homodimers or heterodimers (Accardi, 2015; Stölting et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Accardi, 2015; Stölting et al., 2014).

claim: The C. elegans genome carries 6 ClC genes.
source: The C. elegans genome carries 6 ClC genes (clh-1 through clh-4 for anion channel, and clh-5 and clh-6 for anion transporter, predicted from a key amino acid residue and subcellular localization, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Schriever et al., 1999; Nehrke et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Schriever et al., 1999; Nehrke et al., 2000) and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: clh-1 through clh-4 are predicted to be anion channels.
source: The C. elegans genome carries 6 ClC genes (clh-1 through clh-4 for anion channel, and clh-5 and clh-6 for anion transporter, predicted from a key amino acid residue and subcellular localization, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Schriever et al., 1999; Nehrke et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is based on predictions from amino acid residues and subcellular localization, supported by citations.

claim: clh-5 and clh-6 are predicted to be anion transporters.
source: The C. elegans genome carries 6 ClC genes (clh-1 through clh-4 for anion channel, and clh-5 and clh-6 for anion transporter, predicted from a key amino acid residue and subcellular localization, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Schriever et al., 1999; Nehrke et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is based on predictions from amino acid residues and subcellular localization, supported by citations.

claim: Each single mutant except for clh-5(tm6008) showed normal salt chemotaxis under fed conditions.
source: Food-associated salt chemotaxis was normal in each single (clh-1(tm1243), clh-2(ok636), clh-3(ok763), or clh-4(ok1162)) or clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) double mutants. However, lack of three ClC channels, clh-3(ok763) clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) triple mutation, gave a marked effect on behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) double mutants showed normal salt chemotaxis.
source: Food-associated salt chemotaxis was normal in each single (clh-1(tm1243), clh-2(ok636), clh-3(ok763), or clh-4(ok1162)) or clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) double mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: clh-3(ok763) clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) triple mutation gave a marked effect on salt chemotaxis behavior.
source: However, lack of three ClC channels, clh-3(ok763) clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) triple mutation, gave a marked effect on behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Figure 2b.

claim: The double mutants carrying clh-1(pe572) and a deletion in another clh gene showed a defect similar to that of the clh-1(pe572) single mutant.
source: The double mutants showed a defect similar to that of the clh-1(pe572) single mutant, that is, defective chemotaxis toward low salt.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A hexatruple mutant that carry clh-1(pe572) and a deletion in five other clh genes showed similar phenotype to clh-1(pe572) single mutant.
source: A hexatruple mutant that carry clh-1(pe572) and a deletion in five other clh genes also showed similar phenotype (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Salt chemotaxis defect of clh-1(pe572) mutant is not attributed to impairment of other CLH proteins.
source: These results indicate that salt chemotaxis defect of clh-1(pe572) mutant is not attributed to impairment of other CLH proteins.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the observation that removing other clh genes does not suppress the clh-1(pe572) phenotype.

claim: clh-5(tm6008) and many of the clh multiple mutants that carry clh-5(tm6008) showed high immobility indices.
source: clh-5(tm6008) and many of the clh multiple mutants that carry clh-5(tm6008) showed high immobility indices (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), suggesting that the mutants displayed a locomotion defect on chemotaxis assay plate.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The clh-5(tm6008) mutants displayed a locomotion defect on chemotaxis assay plate.
source: clh-5(tm6008) and many of the clh multiple mutants that carry clh-5(tm6008) showed high immobility indices (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), suggesting that the mutants displayed a locomotion defect on chemotaxis assay plate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high immobility indices observed in these mutants.

claim: Locomotion defects can interfere with chemotaxis of the animals since it prevents prompt migration toward preferred conditions.
source: Locomotion defects can interfere with chemotaxis of the animals since it prevents prompt migration toward preferred conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on logical reasoning about the relationship between locomotion and chemotaxis.

claim: Mutation of clh-3 suppressed locomotion defects in clh-5 clh-3 clh-2 clh-1 quadruple mutants.
source: Actually, mutation of clh-3 partially suppressed chemotaxis defect of the clh-5 clh-2 clh-1 triple mutation (that is, in the clh-5 clh-3 clh-2 clh-1 quadruple mutants) as well as locomotion defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: clh-5 and clh-3 are involved in locomotion upon chemotaxis.
source: These results imply that clh-5 and clh-3 are involved in locomotion upon chemotaxis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the suppression of locomotion defects by clh-3 mutation.

claim: Mutation of clh-6(tm617) V gave rise to salt chemotaxis defect in combination with clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) II mutations.
source: Mutation of clh-6(tm617) V, which encodes a putative anion transporter and whose single mutation had no effect on salt chemotaxis, also gave rise to salt chemotaxis defect in combination with clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) II mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: clh-6 encodes a putative anion transporter.
source: Mutation of clh-6(tm617) V, which encodes a putative anion transporter and whose single mutation had no effect on salt chemotaxis, also gave rise to salt chemotaxis defect in combination with clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) II mutations.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge about clh-6.

claim: clh-6(tm617) single mutation had no effect on salt chemotaxis.
source: Mutation of clh-6(tm617) V, which encodes a putative anion transporter and whose single mutation had no effect on salt chemotaxis, also gave rise to salt chemotaxis defect in combination with clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243) II mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: A hexatruple mutant clh-3(ok763) clh-5(tm6008) clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243); clh-6(tm617); clh-4(ok1162) showed severe defect in both high- and low-salt chemotaxis.
source: Finally, a hexatruple mutant clh-3(ok763) clh-5(tm6008) clh-2(ok636) clh-1(tm1243); clh-6(tm617); clh-4(ok1162) showed severe defect in both high- and low-salt chemotaxis (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: clh genes redundantly act in salt chemotaxis.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that clh genes redundantly act in salt chemotaxis.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the multiple mutant analysis.

claim: Chemotaxis to low salt was more severely affected in clh-1(pe572) hexatruple mutants.
source: It should be noted that chemotaxis to low salt was more severely affected in clh-1(pe572) hexatruple mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The effect of clh-1(pe572) missense mutation is not simply caused by inhibition of other CLH proteins.
source: This further suggests that the effect of clh-1(pe572) missense mutation is not simply caused by inhibition of other CLH proteins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that clh-1(pe572) hexatruple mutants show more severe defects than deletion hexatruple mutants.

claim: clh-1 is expressed in hypodermal cells, seam cells, D-cells of the vulva, and neuronal and glial cells of the head.
source: It has previously been reported that clh-1 is expressed in hypodermal cells, seam cells, D-cells of the vulva, and neuronal and glial cells of the head (Grant et al., 2015; Nehrke et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Grant et al., 2015; Nehrke et al., 2000).

claim: ASE, AWA, and AWC sensory neurons expressed the clh-1 transcriptional reporter.
source: Of the head neurons, at least ASE, AWA, and AWC sensory neurons expressed the reporter (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The mutant phenotype was rescued when clh-1(wt) cDNA was expressed pan-neuronally.
source: The mutant phenotype was rescued when cDNA was expressed either pan-neuronally or specifically in ASER, suggesting that clh-1 acts in the nervous system including ASER (Figure 3b, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a for ASER-specific rescue of pe577).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The mutant phenotype was rescued when clh-1(wt) cDNA was expressed specifically in ASER.
